notes: Tariff '3(2)' against 'identify any three', so bestNofParts — four options displayed, three claimable at 2 each = 6, leaving 4 marks for part (a)(ii) out of the 10 for Q6. Figure p08-i1 opened before writing: the word bank plus the two-by-two photograph grid, all four letters legible and uncut. Letter-to-breed mapping is the scheme's. The scheme spells the breed 'Charolais' here and 'Charollais' in part (ii); this card reproduces the (i) spelling as printed.

questionText: State with reason which cow A or B a farmer would choose to cross with the Belgian Blue bull shown in the picture above.
stem: Answer either (a) or (b). The picture at the head of part (b) — not carried in this crop — shows the Belgian Blue beef breed: an extremely heavily muscled, double-muscled continental bull, white to pale roan in colour. Part (i) asked for two of its physical characteristics.

labelKey.meaning: left — a fawn/tan cow grazing head-down, fine-boned and angular with a large well-filled udder and a pale tail switch
right — a large white-cream cow standing facing the camera, deep and thick through the shoulder and hindquarter with a broad frame

rows.contextNote: The scheme accepts either the letter or the breed name.
Reason — any ONE of the scheme's three reasons scores the 2 marks. All three say the same thing: she is big enough to calve down to a double-muscled bull.

notes: Tariff '2(2)' = the cow (2) plus the reason (2) = 4, fixed. Figure p15-i1 opened before binding and it carries the part (ii) instruction line and both lettered photographs; p15-i2 is a one-pixel-taller duplicate of the same crop and is left unbound so the two do not collide on hash. The bull photograph sits on the same page but in a separate crop (p15-i0), so what it shows is carried in the stem instead — the question's phrase 'shown in the picture above' would otherwise dangle. Reason row keeps the scheme's three solidus alternatives as accepts rather than as extra rows, which would inflate a 4-mark part to 8.

questionText: Briefly outline one reason for your choice in part (i).
stem: Silage making is a very important aspect of farm life as it is an essential feedstuff for ruminant animals on farms. Part (b)(i) printed the two grass photographs below and asked which shows the correct stage of cutting the grass for silage. The marking points here are the ones credited for choosing photograph B; the scheme adds '(Allow opposite points for A)'.

labelKey.meaning: left — a stemmy, pale sward that has run to seed, with many tall stems carrying open branched seed heads standing above the leaves
right — a dense, deep-green sward of broad leaf blades with no stems or seed heads showing

rows.contextNote: One reason only — any ONE of the scheme's three scores the full 2 marks. A candidate who ticked A in part (i) scores by naming the opposite point (stemmy, seed heads out, less digestible).

notes: Flat 2-mark tariff, fixed, one row. The scheme's three solidus alternatives are one point stated three ways and live in accepts. Figure p22-i1 opened before binding: it carries the part (b)(i) instruction and both lettered close-ups, A headed out and B leafy — which is exactly what the reason turns on, so the card cannot stand without it. The same crop is bound by the (b)(iii) card, which is allowed because it is the same figure key. Part (b)(i) itself is skipped: its scheme entry is a bare tick with no answer text.

questionText: Identify the growth stage of plant B by placing a tick (✓) in the correct box. [Inflorescence / Vegetative / Elongation]
stem: Silage making is a very important aspect of farm life as it is an essential feedstuff for ruminant animals on farms. Part (b)(i) printed the two grass photographs below; this part asks about photograph B only. The three options are printed as text boxes on the paper and are reproduced in the question.

labelKey.meaning: left — a stemmy, pale sward that has run to seed, with many tall stems carrying open branched seed heads standing above the leaves
right — a dense, deep-green sward of broad leaf blades with no stems or seed heads showing

rows.contextNote: The box the scheme ticks. Photograph B is all leaf with no stem elongation and no seed head showing, so the sward is still vegetative.

notes: Flat 2-mark tick-box. The three options are TEXT on the paper, so unlike (b)(i) this part has a real answer in the scheme ('Vegetative') and is fully cardable; the options are transcribed into questionText as printed. The figure is still needed because 'plant B' is a dangling reference without it — p22-i1 was opened and carries both lettered photographs. Letter A is decoded but marked not-asked, so the student still leaves with the whole figure read.

questionText: Label the diagram of the ewe reproductive system using the list of words in the box below.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). The breeding season is an important and busy time on sheep farms to ensure successful lamb production. Part (a)(i) asked about the management of the ewe at mating. All four lettered parts are to be labelled here, from the word bank Ovary, Uterus, Fallopian tube, Cervix.

labelKey.meaning: arrow into the thick pink horn-shaped structure at the top left of the tract, the body and horns seen from the front
arrow to the fine coiled tube at the outer end of the left horn, just before the small pale round body
arrow to the small pale round body at the outer end of the right horn
arrow to the narrow ridged neck on the midline, where the body of the tract narrows into the passage below it

notes: Tariff '4(3)' = four labels at 3 marks each = 12, and the question asks for all four (not 'any three'), so this is fixed, not bestNofParts — the rows sum exactly to the tariff. Figure p25-i1 opened before binding: the front-view illustration with four blue leader arrows and the word bank beside it, all four letters legible. Letter-to-part mapping is the scheme's own; the label key describes only where each arrow lands. Note the scheme heads this part 'the female reproductive system' while the paper prints 'the ewe reproductive system' — the paper's wording is used for questionText.

questionText: Using the colours in the box below, list the colours in order of sequence used by the farmer during mating.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). At mating the farmer straps a raddle on the ram to mark the ewes that have been served, and part (b)(iii) established that the colour is changed every 13–15 days so that any ewe repeating shows up. The answer table on the paper has three rows: 1st colour, 2nd colour, 3rd colour. The scheme accepts either the colour name or the letter of the tub.

labelKey.meaning: left — a 1 kg tub of pale green raddle powder
centre — a 1 kg tub of pale blue raddle powder
right — a 1 kg tub of pale yellow raddle powder

rows.contextNote: The sequence runs lightest to darkest so that each new mark shows up over the one before it.

notes: The scheme prints the tariff as '4 + 1 + 1' for a 6-mark part without saying which colour carries which value — under the scheme's own front matter the FIRST correct answer encountered takes the 4 — so this is orderedSplit and every row is marks: null. Putting 4/1/1 on specific rows would be a claim the scheme does not make. Figure p26-i0 opened before binding: three identical 1 kg raddle tubs headed A (green), B (blue), C (yellow), which is what makes the scheme's 'Yellow / C' pairing readable. The solidus in each row separates two wordings of one answer (the colour or its letter), not two marking points.

questionText: Identify the breed of dairy cow shown in the picture below.
stem: Answer both (a) and (b) with either (c) or (d). Calving is a very busy time on all beef and dairy farms, so it is important for farmers to be prepared in advance. Parts (a)(i) and (a)(ii) dealt with preparing for the calving season and with the practices carried out on the calf at birth.

rows.contextNote: The brackets are the scheme's: 'Friesian' alone is enough, and 'Holstein Friesian' is equally acceptable.

notes: Flat 6-mark tariff, one answer, fixed. Figure p34-i0 opened before binding: the part (iii) instruction line above a single photograph of a black-and-white cow grazing, lean and angular with a large udder — no letters on it, so the card carries a figure with an empty label key and stays a question card rather than a diagram card. Nothing in the photograph is cut.

questionText: Identify the hormone labelled X responsible for milk let down.
stem: Question 13, part (d) — answered instead of part (c). The paper prints: 'A hormone is responsible for milk let down in cows. Analyse the picture and answer the questions that follow.' The picture below is that picture. Part (ii), printed under the same picture, then asks for one trigger of milk let down.

labelKey.meaning: Oxytocin

notes: Figure opened before writing (public/exam-figures/agricultural-science/markbank/agricultural-science-2025-HL-paper-p24-i0.png): a cut-out side view of a black-and-white Holstein Friesian facing right, with a red pathway overlaid — a solid red dot high on the head behind the poll, a heavy red dashed line running down the neck to a point at the shoulder, then back horizontally along the underline, then down to a red arrowhead at the udder. A blue-outlined label box reading 'Hormone X' sits lower right with a solid red arrow pointing at the shoulder bend of that pathway. Parts (i) and (ii) with their blank answer boxes are printed beneath the picture on the same crop, so the student sees the question exactly as the paper set it. Scheme p.18 prints a single answer, 'Oxytocin', against the full 5 marks — one row, fixed tariff, no solidus and no alternatives to split. labelKey decodes X so the build's lettered-parts guard is satisfied; askedInThisQuestion is true because X is precisely what this part asks for, which also keeps the 'Also on the diagram' panel from printing the answer. The companion card agsci-2025-hl-q13dii (part (ii), milk let-down triggers) already exists and carries no figure, so this crop is bound exactly once in the subject deck.

questionText: Identify A and B in the chart above of the composition of milk.
stem: Question 15, part (b). A north Clare dairy farm sells its value-added milk to local people through a milk vending machine, and to produce milk for human consumption it must be of the highest standard. The chart shows the typical composition of cow's milk. Its five sectors carry the values 3.40%, 4.00%, 87.5%, 4.20% and 0.90%; the legend names three of them — Protein, Lactose and Minerals — and leaves the other two lettered A and B. The paper's answer table has one column, Component, with a row for A and a row for B.

labelKey.meaning: The 4.00% sector, drawn in purple and pulled out from the pie — (butter) fat.
The large green 87.5% sector that forms the body of the pie — water.

rows.contextNote: The bracketed word is context, not a requirement — "fat" scores.

notes: Figure opened and checked by eye: agricultural-science-2025-OL-paper-p25-i0.png is this part's own exploded pie, titled "Average Milk Composition", with the red bold B inside the 87.5% green sector and the white A on the 4.00% purple sector, the legend listing Protein, A, B, Lactose and Minerals, and the Component answer table underneath. The percentages extract as text but which value carries A and which carries B is only readable from the chart, so the crop is what makes the part answerable. Tariff: the scheme prints a single combined "4+2" against the A and B lines, so no per-row value is claimed — same treatment as sibling part (b)(ii), whose "5+2" was also modelled as an ordered split. Q15 reconciles as 13 (part a) + 12 + 7 + 6 (part b) + 12 (part c) = 50.

questionText: Identify one way in which the farm in the photograph could become more energy efficient.
stem: Question 4 opens "Study the photograph of the farm layout below and answer the questions which follow." Beneath that line the paper prints one oblique aerial colour photograph of a working Irish farmyard — house, sheds, yard, storage and the surrounding grass fields — and all three parts of Question 4 are answered from that single photograph. The crop stops after the printed text of this part, so parts (b) and (c) are not shown. Question 4 is worth 10 marks; this part carries 2.

rows.verbatim: Solar panels / increase amount of roof lights or sky lights or reduce the need for artificial light / install windmill / install bio‐digester
rows.contextNote: One 2-mark point; every alternative the scheme separates with a solidus is a different way of earning the same 2. The scheme's list is not closed — it ends with the examiner instruction "other valid answer" — so a sensible energy measure you can justify from this yard scores even though it is not printed. That permission is what openList records here.

notes: Figure opened and checked: agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p08-i0.png is the Question 4 aerial farmyard photograph together with its heading and the printed text of part (a). The question says "the farm in the photograph", so it is a dangling reference without the crop. One row: the scheme prints a single 2 for the whole list, and openList is set because the scheme itself ends with "other valid answer" — that phrase is an examiner instruction, not a wording a candidate could write, so it is encoded by openList alone and is no longer carried in accepts. The only remaining accepts entry is the scheme's own fifth alternative, "rainwater harvesting". The stem was also cut back to context — where the question sits, what kind of image it is, the tariff — because its earlier inventory of the yard called out the shed's rooflights, which is one of the scheme's own marking points.

questionText: State two ways in which the farmyard is suited to economy of labour.
stem: Question 4 continued, answered from the same aerial photograph of the farm layout printed at the head of the question. The crop bound to this card carries the photograph and, beneath it, the printed text of part (a) — a separate part asking about energy efficiency — because parts (b) and (c) are printed below the crop's bottom edge. Read the layout of the yard off the photograph yourself. This part carries 4 of the question's 10 marks.

rows.contextNote: The scheme prints 2(2): any TWO of its six observations score, 2 marks each. Two of the six are displayed as rows; the other four are carried in accepts on both rows, and neither displayed row's own wording appears in the other's accepts — a point can only be claimed once.
accepts: farmyard is located close to main house
sheds are well designed for machinery access

rows.verbatim: silage bales and pit are located close to the sheds
accepts: farmyard is located close to main house
sheds are well designed for machinery access

notes: Bound to the inspected Question 4 crop agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p08-i0.png. Every answer the scheme allows is an observation read off that photograph — sheds close together, bales and pit beside the sheds, cow housing close to the parlour — so the part is unmarkable without it. Modelled as fixed 2(2) with two displayed rows at 2 each and the remaining four of the scheme's six options in accepts on both rows. Both displayed verbatims are now excluded from the shared accepts pool, matching the file's existing fixed 2(2) precedent at 2021 HL Q2(a)(iii); previously each row's accepts held the other row's verbatim, which let a single scheme option be self-awarded on both rows for 4 marks where the scheme awards 2. bestNofParts is not used because only two rows are displayed and a student can claim both. The stem was also cut back to context: it previously described the house above the yard, the sheds adjoining each other, the bales beside the sheds and the roadways to the fields — four of the six marking points, handed over before the student answered.

questionText: What is meant by this farm safety sign?
stem: Question 8 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (a)(ii). Part (a) opens: 'As part of the Bord Bia Quality Assurance Schemes, farmers must ensure that all of their medicines are locked away in a medicine cabinet', and (a)(i) asked why. The sign this part asks about is printed on its own in the right-hand margin beside the (a)(ii) answer box — a yellow triangular warning sign with a heavy black border and a single black pictogram inside it. The photograph of an open medicine cabinet higher up the crop belongs to part (a)(i), not to this part.

rows.contextNote: The solidi separate three wordings of ONE 2-mark point — the sign has one meaning, and any one of the three carries the whole 2. A second, wrong meaning written beside a right one cancels the mark.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p10-i0 shows the Question 8 choice line, the part (a) stem, the (a)(i) answer box with its medicine-cabinet photograph, the (a)(ii) instruction and the yellow triangular sign in the right margin, whole and untruncated. The stem says plainly which image belongs to which part so the student is not left guessing. Bound because the whole question is 'what does THIS sign mean'. The scheme's third wording, 'electric shock risk', is now in accepts; it cannot be the row verbatim because the scheme file typesets the marks cell inside it ('… / electric 2' then 'shock risk'), which I checked against the file — but accepts is not traceability-checked, so there was never a reason to withhold it. The stem describes the sign as a yellow triangle with a black pictogram rather than naming the pictogram, since naming it is most of the answer. Part (b)(i) asks about a DIFFERENT sign on page 11 with a different answer ('Caution farm machinery'); no p11 crop exists on disk (verified), so that part is skipped rather than bound to this one.

questionText: Outline the function of the part labelled A.
stem: Question 10 prints a side-view line drawing of the reproductive system of a cow, with the bladder and the vulva named on the drawing and one further structure picked out by a short red arrow labelled A. Part (a) asked you to name A. The scheme scores (a) and (b) as separate 2-mark points, so this mark does not depend on having named A correctly — describe what the structure the arrow points to does.

labelKey.meaning: the short red arrow left of centre. It points to the small oval body at the tip of the coiled horn on the left of the drawing — the structure whose function this part asks for.

rows.verbatim: (Produces) eggs or ovulation or produces oestrogen
rows.contextNote: Four alternatives for ONE 2-mark point: produces eggs, ovulation, produces oestrogen, or produces progesterone. Any single one carries the whole 2 — the 'or's are alternatives, not separate marks.

notes: Figure opened and verified: agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p13-i0 shows the whole drawing, the red A arrow, the Bladder and Vulva callouts and the (a), (b) and (c) instructions. Bound because 'the part labelled A' means nothing without the drawing. The scheme's fourth alternative, progesterone, is now claimable through accepts; it cannot be appended to the row verbatim because the scheme file typesets the marks cell inside the phrase ('… produces oestrogen or 2' then 'progesterone'), which I confirmed against the file and against the build's traceability check — accepts is not traceability-checked, so the wording belongs there. The label key no longer names the structure: part (a) on the same figure asks the student to name it and this part asks what it does, so naming it in the key would hand over both.

questionText: Outline one way in which the farmyard layout is economically sustainable.
stem: Question 11 offers a choice of (a) or (b); this is part (a)(iii). The figure is a 3D aerial render of a farmyard set in open fields. The paper labels two features on it — 'Cow cubicle house' and 'Dairy cow collecting yard' — and a red pointer picks out a third as B, which parts (a)(i) and (a)(ii) asked about. This part steps back to the layout as a whole: one observation is wanted, and the marks are for something you can read off the render.

labelKey.meaning: the red pointer entering from the right-hand edge of the render. It aims at the long, low bays between concrete walls whose covers are held down by a dense scatter of dark round weights. Parts (a)(i) and (a)(ii) ask about B; this part does not.

accepts: good access roads through the farm
rows.contextNote: Three wordings of ONE 2-mark point, and the scheme then adds 'other valid answer' — so a different observation read off this layout can also score. That is why this row is an open list: self-marking here is a judgement about whether what you wrote is a real economic-sustainability feature of the layout, not a lookup.

questionText: Identify the best quality silage and state for which animals this silage is suitable.
stem: Question 6, part (a)(ii). Question 6 offers (a) or (b); this is the (a) route, and part (i) has already asked about the letters BCS that run through the captions. The diagram shows the grass growth cycle and how each growth stage affects silage quality: five drawings of a grass plant run left to right from a short leafy tuft to a tall stem that has headed out, an orange bar beneath them carries the letters A, B, C and D, and under that the row labelled 'Silage % Dry Matter Digestibility (DMD)' brackets a band of DMD figures beneath each letter together with the class of animal that band suits. The paper prints two answer lines, 'Silage quality:' and 'Animal:'.

labelKey.meaning: the first bracket from the left in the 'Silage % Dry Matter Digestibility (DMD)' row, sitting at the young, leafy end of the growth cycle; the only one of the four brackets that spans two DMD columns, and it carries a single animal caption
the second bracket, one DMD column wide, with a single animal caption
the third bracket, one DMD column wide, carrying two animal captions
the fourth and rightmost bracket, at the mature, stemmy, headed-out end of the growth cycle; one DMD column wide, carrying two animal captions

rows.verbatim: Best quality silage = 76%+ DMD or A
rows.contextNote: The scheme's "or" gives two ways of naming one band — the DMD figure or the letter — so either alone takes the 2. Quality falls left to right as the grass matures, so the best silage comes from the leafiest, least mature grass; on the chart that bracket is the only one spanning two DMD columns, and its upper column is the top of the scale.

rows.verbatim: Suitable animals = freshly calved dairy cows in winter milk
rows.contextNote: This is the caption the paper prints under the band named in the first row, and it has to match that band — reading the animals off a neighbouring bracket loses this mark even if the band itself was named correctly.
